A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GaussRender. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original training and evaluation results for GaussRender across three occupancy datasets, including benchmark comparisons, rendering metrics and ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark results and reports additional RayIoU evaluations, loss-component ablations, sensitivity studies and qualitative predictions.

M1.justification: The voxel-to-Gaussian architecture and rendering approach remain. However, v1 explicitly excludes BeV depth supervision, whereas v2 includes it in the rendering objective (Eqs. 4–6), supported by Table 5. V2 also introduces maximum-depth normalization into the stated depth loss.

E1.justification: Both versions train and evaluate on SurroundOcc-nuScenes, Occ3D-nuScenes and SSCBench-KITTI360 for the same driving-scene occupancy tasks. Added metrics, ablations and qualitative examples remain within this coverage; virtual-camera variations change supervision procedures rather than the input task.

E2.justification: V2 adds RayIoU comparisons including BEVDet-Occ, BEVDet-Occ-Long, SparseOcc and FB-Occ. V1's standalone 2D-only comparison against SelfOcc, GaussianOcc, RenderOcc and GSRender disappears. Table 1 adds GSRender at 29.56 mIoU and removes the RenderOcc lidar-only row at 23.93, although that row remains in Appendix E; the 26.11 RenderOcc entry is retained.

E3.justification: V2 replaces sensor-view image/depth evaluation with RayIoU at 1, 2 and 4 meter tolerances while retaining BeV evaluation. Reported camera elevation changes from 8 to 2 meters, random translation changes from ±10 meters to half the maximum range, and the selected loss weight changes from 5 to 15. The Gaussian-scale sweep also changes. These documented revisions do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds incremental loss-component ablation (Table 5), loss-weight and camera-count sensitivity studies (Appendix D), and qualitative prediction examples. The viewpoint study gains stereo and elevated-plus-random strategies. Gaussian-scale analysis is retained, relocated and revised, rather than newly introduced. V1's standalone experiment comparing models trained only with 2D supervision is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, empirical error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. The additional curves retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Main GaussRender benchmark scores and all per-class numerical rows are unchanged. V2 adds RayIoU results, including TPVFormer at 37.2 without and 38.3 with GaussRender, and SurroundOcc at 35.5 and 37.5. BeV values are revised, camera/scale-ablation results are replaced under revised documented settings, and new sensitivity results appear. Sensor-view scores and the 2D-only comparison disappear. Appendix C newly reports 17% faster attainment of baseline performance.

T1.justification: V2 revises the mathematical rendering-loss definition through depth normalization and inclusion of BeV depth. It also explicitly defines projected Gaussian covariance and depth compositing in Eqs. 2–3, beyond v1's covariance and semantic-compositing equations. Neither version presents theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The architecture-independent rendering-loss contribution and three-benchmark success claim remain. V2 adds an explicit main claim of leading performance on surface-sensitive metrics and changes v1's characterization of a single degree of freedom to a few loosely sensitive hyperparameters.

C2.justification: V2 explains how thick or duplicated surfaces can inflate voxel IoU and motivates RayIoU accordingly. Appendix D adds interpretations of excessive versus insufficient rendering-loss weight and the limited benefit of additional cameras. Appendix C newly argues that faster learning outweighs per-iteration overhead. Existing explanations of occlusion handling and Gaussian-scale failure modes largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies fixed 20% training/validation subsets for ablations and gives more explicit camera-selection and parameter instructions. It updates loss-weight information and adds a statement about available qualitative GIFs, but removes v1's explicit identification of the retrained SurroundOcc baselines. Optimizer, training duration, hardware information and the code-access address remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 removes extensive general NeRF and Gaussian editing, physics and generation references, while adding works including GaussTR, SparseOcc, BEVDet4D, POP3D and OccFeat. Related work is substantially refocused on occupancy representations and rendering supervision, with expanded distinctions concerning architectural coupling, foundation models and temporal supervision.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Section 3 is reorganized around consistency, camera placement, rendering and loss computation. Gaussian-scale analysis moves into an expanded ablation appendix, and a qualitative-results appendix is added. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the opening performance graphic with an artifact comparison, removes earlier explanatory cartoons, consolidates the pipeline and Gaussianization diagrams, and redraws camera positioning. It adds RayIoU and loss-component tables, sensitivity plots and full-page qualitative figures. The former multi-view results table is reduced to BeV columns, while the scale study is relocated and replotted.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens support for spatial consistency through RayIoU evaluation, loss-component ablation and sensitivity studies, while clearer diagrams improve assessability. The net gain is limited by removal of the 2D-only comparison and sensor-view evidence. Core benchmark results remain unchanged, and Appendix C's new 17%-faster learning claim lacks an accompanying convergence analysis. Overall, the additional targeted evidence supports a modest improvement.
